newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish unions, employers tackle labour reform.
newsitem.headline: Spanish unions, employers tackle labour reform.

text.p: Spanish unions and employers began talks on Monday aimed at liberalising one of Europe's most rigid labour markets, under government pressure to produce a deal preparing the economy for European monetary union. But analysts fear that reforms will not go far enough before the single European currency is launched in 1999, when the government's room for manoeuvre will be greatly restricted.
"This will be the first step, but labour regulations still have a long way to go to catch up with the rest of Europe," said Juan Antonio Mielgo, economist at Bank of America in Madrid.

The government has given unions and employers the first few weeks of 1997 to come to a preliminary agreement, and has threatened to legislate if an agreement is not reached or if the pact is not radical enough.

In the past, Spain has used peseta devaluations to cushion any loss of competitive edge in downturns. But that recourse would no longer exist once a common currency is established under Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Economists believe unions and employers are likely to reach an agreement but it may take some prodding from the government.

"From a political standpoint the government needs to stay out of the talks due to the sensitivity of the issues concerned such as firing," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
"However, the government will probably nudge them, but from behind the curtains," he added.
Analysts said that if reforms were not far reaching enough by the time Spain entered EMU, the economy would suffer and unemployment could worsen.

"The labour market will be a key factor in EMU, because countries will no longer be able to compete with exchange rates, or monetary or fiscal policy, and can only compete with labour market flexibility and competitiveness," said Mielgo.

Shortly after taking office last year, Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said his priority was to reach a German-style jobs pact with unions to help tackle Spain's towering unemployment, currently the worst in Europe at around 22 percent.
The previous Socialist administration took one step toward liberalising the market in 1994, introducing new specialised contracts for apprenticeships and temporary work.
But detractors say the changes institutionalised the split between permanent and temporary work, and left unresolved the issue of high dismissal costs.
One in three employees are on temporary contracts in Spain, almost twice as many as in the rest of the European Union.
Analysts said unions and employers needed to agree on two key areas: developing more stable contracts and easing restrictions on firing workers. But this will not be easy.

The government's relationship with unions and employers is far from easy. Aznar's Popular Party upset unions by calling a freeze on public-sector wages in 1997 needed to help whip the country's finances into shape for EMU.
The move prompted a 24-hour strike in December and unions say they would not back down until the government relents.
The government also upset employers with a pensions deal which they denounced as overgenerous and refused to sign.
